--- title: "Highlighting parts of the Chart" subtitle: "" date: 2025/8/30 date-modified: "2025-09-03" order: 40 --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(ggformula) library(systemfonts) ## use custom fonts (need to be installed on your OS) library(paletteer) ## access to many color palettes library(showtext) ## add google fonts to plots library(ggtext) ## add improved text rendering to ggplot2 ## library(ggforce) ## add missing functionality to ggplot2 library(concaveman) # for convex hulls with ggforce library(ggfocus) # Scales which help add emphasis to *any* geom! library(gghighlight) ## highlight parts of ggplot2 plots ``` ::: ## Introduction We may have been using `ggplot2` for a while now, but there is always more to learn about the aesthetics of our plots. Here we will look at ways to highlight specific areas of our plots, to draw attention to them. We will introduce three packages that can help us do this: `ggfocus`, `ggforce`, and `gghighlight`. ### Fonts and Themes As we learnt in the [Fonts Module](../20-Fonts/index.qmd), let us set the ggplot theme with fonts for both the chart defining elements **and** our annotations. I am going to use local fonts from my machine, that I have downloaded from Google Fonts earlier and saved in a `fonts` folder at the root of my project. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ## Clean the slate systemfonts::clear_local_fonts() systemfonts::clear_registry() ## showtext_opts(dpi = 96) # set DPI for showtext sysfonts::font_add( family = "Alegreya", regular = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Regular.ttf", bold = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Bold.ttf", italic = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Italic.ttf", bolditalic = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-BoldItalic.ttf" ) sysfonts::font_add( family = "Anton", regular = "../../../../../../fonts/Anton-Regular.ttf" ) # Only one style is available sysfonts::font_add( family = "RobotoCondensed", regular = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Regular.ttf", bold = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Bold.ttf", italic = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Italic.ttf", bolditalic = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-BoldItalic.ttf" ) sysfonts::font_add( family = "IbarraNova", regular = "../../../../../../fonts/IbarraRealNova-Regular.ttf", bold = "../../../../../../fonts/IbarraRealNova-Bold.ttf", italic = "../../../../../../fonts/IbarraRealNova-Italic.ttf", bolditalic = "../../../../../../fonts/IbarraRealNova-BoldItalic.ttf" ) sysfonts::font_add( family = "Tangerine", regular = "../../../../../../fonts/Tangerine-Regular.ttf", bold = "../../../../../../fonts/Tangerine-Bold.ttf" ) # only these two are available sysfonts::font_add( family = "Schoolbell", regular = "../../../../../../fonts/Schoolbell-Regular.ttf" ) # Only regular is available showtext_auto() # set these fonts as default for the session ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} theme_custom <- function() { font <- "RobotoCondensed" # Assign font family up front theme_bw(base_size = 14, base_family = font) %+replace% ## modify plot elements globally (for all following plots) theme( axis.ticks = element_line(color = "grey92"), axis.ticks.length = unit(.5, "lines"), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.title = element_text(family = "Schoolbell", size = 12), legend.text = element_text(family = "IbarraNova", color = "grey30"), plot.title = element_text( # title family = "Alegreya", # set font family size = 18, # set font size face = "bold", # bold typeface hjust = 0, # left align margin = margin(t = 5, r = 0, b = 5, l = 0) ), # margin plot.title.position = "plot", plot.subtitle = element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 12, color = "grey30", hjust = 0, # left align margin = margin(t = 5, r = 0, b = 10, l = 0) ), # margin plot.caption = element_text( # caption family = font, # font family size = 9, # font size hjust = 1 ), # right align plot.caption.position = "plot", # right align to plot ) } ## Set the theme ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) ## Use available fonts in ggplot text geoms too! ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "text", new = list( family = "RobotoCondensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" )) ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "label", new = list( family = "RobotoCondensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" )) ``` ::: ## Data We will again work with a **familiar** dataset, so that we can concentrate on the chart aesthetics, without having to spend time getting used to the data: the `penguins` dataset again, ~~from the `palmerpenguins` package~~ now part of the R installation! As always, we will start with a **table** of the data: ::: {#tbl-read-penguins-data .cell tbl-cap='Penguins Dataset'} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} penguins <- penguins %>% drop_na() # remove data containing missing data ## Create a nicely formatted table ## uses `kableExtra` package ## penguins %>% kableExtra::kbl(caption = "Penguins Dataset") %>% kableExtra::kable_paper( full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"), position = "center" ) %>% kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "350px") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ## Basic Plots A basic scatter plot, which we will use to highlight and draw attention to specific areas of the plot. We will include, for the sake of retaining context, the fonts and labels that we have used in previous modules. And we will also use `ggtext` to format the axis titles and the plot title. We will colour one plot using a **Quant** variable, and the other using a **Qual** variable, to show that the highlighting methods work with both types of variables. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} p1 <- gf_point( data = penguins, bill_dep ~ bill_len, color = ~body_mass, alpha = 0.8, size = 3.5 ) %>% ## custom colors from the scico package gf_refine(scico::scale_color_scico(palette = "tokyo", direction = -1)) %>% ## custom labels gf_labs( title = "Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins (**Pygoscelis**)", subtitle = "A scatter plot of bill depth versus bill length.", caption = "Data: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014) PLoS ONE", x = "**Bill Length** (mm)", y = "**Bill Depth** (mm)", color = "Body mass (g)" ) %>% ## 2. Add theme related commands from ggtext ## render respective text elements gf_theme(theme( plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(), plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown() )) p1 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Basic Scatter Plot coloured by Body Mass](index_files/figure-html/fig-basic-ggformula-scatter-1.png){#fig-basic-ggformula-scatter width=2100} ::: ::: And another scatter plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} p2 <- ggplot(penguins, aes( x = bill_len, y = bill_dep, colour = species )) + geom_point(size = 3.5) + # Add colours scale_color_paletteer_d("ggsci::category10_d3") + # Add labels labs( title = "Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins (*Pygoscelis*)", subtitle = "A scatter plot of bill depth versus bill length.", caption = "Data: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014) *PLoS ONE*", x = "**Bill Length** (mm)", y = "**Bill Depth** (mm)", color = "Body mass (g)", fill = "Species" ) + ## 2. Add theme related commands from ggtext ## render respective text elements gf_theme(theme( plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(), plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown() )) p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Basic Scatter Plot coloured by Species](index_files/figure-html/fig-basic-ggplot2-scatter-1.png){#fig-basic-ggplot2-scatter width=2100} ::: ::: ## Using `{ggfocus}` `ggfocus` provides ***scales*** which help add emphasis to *any* geom! It works by fading out the non-focused data, and can be used with any geom, including those from other packages. It is particularly useful for highlighting points in scatter plots, lines in line plots, or bars in bar plots. Some examples of these scales are: - `scale_focus_color()`: Highlights points based on a condition, changing their color and adjusting the transparency of non-highlighted points. - `scale_focus_fill()`: for filled geoms like bars or areas. - `scale_focus_size()`: adjusts the size of the highlighted points instead of color. - `scale_focus_alpha()`: Adjusts the transparency of points based on a condition, making non-highlighted points more transparent. - `scale_focus_linetype()`: Highlights lines in line plots based on a condition by changing their linetype and adjusting the transparency of non-highlighted lines. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p2 + ggfocus::scale_color_focus( focus_levels = c("Gentoo"), color_focus = "red", # color for highlighted points color_other = "grey80", # color for non-highlighted points ) + labs(subtitle = "Highlighting Gentoo Penguins using ggfocus") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Using `ggfocus` to highlight points in a scatter plot](index_files/figure-html/fig-ggfocus-example-1.png){#fig-ggfocus-example width=2100} ::: ::: We can also highlight for `fill`, using the `ggformula` idiom this time: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gf_histogram(~body_mass, data = penguins, fill = ~species) %>% gf_refine(ggfocus::scale_fill_focus( focus_levels = c("Gentoo"), # condition to highlight points color_focus = "dodgerblue", # color for highlighted points color_other = "grey80", # color for non-highlighted points )) %>% gf_labs( title = "Penguins Body Mass Histograms", subtitle = "Highlighting Gentoo Penguins using ggfocus" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Using `ggfocus` to highlight points in a histogram based on a categorical condition](index_files/figure-html/fig-ggfocus-example-2-1.png){#fig-ggfocus-example-2 width=2100} ::: ::: We see that the scales from `ggfocus` directly use the ***existing*** aesthetics of the plot, and modify them to highlight specific data points. This is different from the other two packages we will see, which add new geoms to the plot to create the highlighting effect. ## Using `{ggforce}` From [Thomas Lin Pedersen's website](www.ggforce.data-imaginist.com) → www.ggforce.data-imaginist.com > `ggforce` is a package aimed at providing missing functionality to `ggplot2` through the extension system introduced with `ggplot2` v2.0.0. Broadly speaking `ggplot2` has been aimed primarily at explorative data visualization in order to investigate the data at hand, and less at providing utilities for composing custom plots a la `D3.js`. `ggforce` is mainly an attempt to address these “shortcomings” (design choices might be a better description). The goal is to provide a repository of geoms, stats, etc. that are as well documented and implemented as the official ones found in `ggplot2`. `ggforce` provides several ways to highlight specific areas of a plot, including `ellipses`, `circles`, `rectangles`, and `convex hulls`. These can be used to draw attention to specific groups or clusters of points in a scatter plot. It also allows highlighting using a *different aesthetic* than the one used in the main plot, as we shall see. This was not possible with the simple-to-use scales of `ggfocus`. Both are useful!!! ### Using ellipses We can highlight *all groups* within a dataset using ellipses: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 + # penguins data is inherited automatically # Can use other data also if needed ggforce::geom_mark_ellipse( aes( fill = species, # Note the variable used here!! label = species ), alpha = .15, show.legend = FALSE ) + # Repeat the points! # Why? So the ellipses don't hide them! geom_point(aes(color = body_mass), # And note Colour variable used here! alpha = .6, size = 3.5 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Ellipses for all groups](index_files/figure-html/fig-ellipses-1.png){#fig-ellipses width=2100} ::: ::: ### Highlighting one group `ggforce`, being ***data-aware*** ( it *inherits* the data too, and not just the plot!) allows us to highlight a specific group within the data, using the `filter` aesthetic. This is very useful when we want to draw attention to a specific subset of the data. #### Add an Ellipse ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## ellipsoids for specific subset p1 + ggforce::geom_mark_ellipse( aes( fill = species, label = species, filter = species == "Gentoo" ), # Very Curious syntax here!! alpha = 0.25, show.legend = FALSE ) + geom_point(aes(color = body_mass), alpha = .6, size = 3.5 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Highlighting one group with an ellipse](index_files/figure-html/fig-ellipse-one-group-1.png){#fig-ellipse-one-group width=2100} ::: ::: #### Adding Circles ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 + ggforce::geom_mark_circle( aes( fill = species, label = species, filter = species == "Gentoo" ), alpha = 0.25, show.legend = FALSE ) + geom_point(aes(color = body_mass), alpha = .6, size = 3.5 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Highlighting one group with circles](index_files/figure-html/fig-circles-one-group-1.png){#fig-circles-one-group width=2100} ::: ::: #### Adding Rectangles ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 + ggforce::geom_mark_rect( aes( fill = species, label = species, filter = species == "Gentoo" ), alpha = 0.25, show.legend = FALSE ) + geom_point(aes(color = body_mass), alpha = .6, size = 3.5 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Highlighting one group with rectangles](index_files/figure-html/fig-rectangles-one-group-1.png){#fig-rectangles-one-group width=2100} ::: ::: #### Adding a Convex Hull A ***convex hull*** is the smallest convex shape that can enclose a set of points. Imagine stretching a rubber band around the outermost points in a scatter plot; the shape formed by the rubber band is the convex hull. It effectively captures the boundary of the data points, providing a visual representation of their spread and extent. `ggforce` uses another package called `concaveman` to compute the convex hulls. This package implements a fast algorithm for computing concave hulls, which can be more representative of the data shape than convex hulls, especially for irregularly distributed points. ::: callout-note ### Highlighting using a different `aesthetic` The `filter` aesthetic in `ggforce::geom_mark_*` functions is used to specify which subset of the data should be highlighted or marked. It allows you to apply a condition to filter the data points that will be enclosed by the marking shape (like ellipse, circle, rectangle, or convex hull). With the original graph `p1`, we have coloured using `body_mass`, but here we are filtering using `species`. This shows that the `filter` aesthetic can be used independently of the aesthetics used in the main plot, allowing for flexible and targeted highlighting of specific data subsets. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # library(concaveman) ## hull p1 + ggforce::geom_mark_hull( aes( fill = species, label = species, filter = species == "Gentoo" ), alpha = 0.25, show.legend = FALSE ) + geom_point(aes(color = body_mass), alpha = .6, size = 3.5 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Highlighting one group with a convex hull](index_files/figure-html/fig-hull-one-group-1.png){#fig-hull-one-group width=2100} ::: ::: In summary, `ggforce` provides a powerful and flexible way to highlight specific areas of a plot using various shapes. The ability to use a different aesthetic for filtering allows for targeted emphasis on particular data subsets, enhancing the interpretability of the visualizations. ## Using `{gghighlight}` To be Written Up. ## {{< iconify ooui references-ltr >}} References 1. ::: {#refs style="font-size: 60%;"} ###### {{< iconify lucide package-check >}} R Package Citations ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in cite_packages(output = "table", out.dir = ".", out.format = "html", : could not find function "cite_packages" ``` ::: ::: :::
